name: Torque to hp
seoTitle: Torque to hp Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Torque to hp: work out speed from the torque and the horsepower. A free conversion calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Torque to hp calculator turns the torque and the horsepower into speed. It is built for a recipe, a shopping list, a travel plan or a form that asks for a unit you do not use. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the Torque to hp calculator work?
sections.html:
The Torque to hp calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports speed in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the torque and the horsepower.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in newton meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 18 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in mechanical horsepowers. The unit chip switches it to any of the 21 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Torque to hp calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Speed=(5968 ÷ 625) × power ÷ torque
Power=horsepower

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Torque = 10 N·m and Power = 10 kW. The calculator returns Speed = 9.5488 rpm and Horsepower = 10 hp(l).

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Speed = 9.5488 rpm and Horsepower = 10 hp(l) should be roughly the size you expected from Torque = 10 N·m and Power = 10 kW.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in rotations per minute, and convertible to any of the 3 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilowatts, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Torque, opening in newton meters
  • Rotational speed, opening in rotations per minute
  • Power, opening in kilowatts
  • Power, opening in mechanical horsepowers

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Torque to hp calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a product listing against the measurements you work with
  • Reading a recipe written in units you do not use
  • Converting a figure someone quoted you so you can compare it
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the torque and the horsepower — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Torque to hp calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Torque to hp calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns speed, derived from the torque and the horsepower. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Torque to hp calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the torque and the horsepower, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter torque in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Torque opens in newton meters and the chip beside it offers 18 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Speed = 9.5488 rpm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Torque to hp calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
